rule: Next 10 claims by testability for each of Darwin and Thompson after the 20 used in experiment 1, excluding claims with a claim-tests directory, claims in holdout/exam.json claims_mentioning_holdout or holdout/burned.json, and any claim whose label, statement or quote contains a bird word (regex in swarm/compare/select2.log). Ties by id. Frozen before any experiment-2 run.

claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
claims.statement: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.
claims.quote: Notwithstanding such modifications, we might expect still to see in the cave-animals of America, affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent, and in those of Europe, to the inhabitants of the European continent.

claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
claims.statement: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.
claims.quote: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.

claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
claims.statement: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.
claims.quote: the first great fact which strikes us is, that neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of various regions can be accounted for by their climatal and other physical conditions.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
claims.statement: Fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other than fossils from two formations widely separated in time, and the fauna of each period is broadly intermediate between those before and after it.
claims.quote: fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other, than are the fossils from two remote formations.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Oceans and continents have kept roughly their present positions since the Silurian
claims.statement: Since no oceanic island bears Palaeozoic or Secondary formations, oceans have probably occupied their present areas, and continents theirs, since the earliest Silurian period, though the arrangement may have differed long before.
claims.quote: we may infer that where our oceans now extend, oceans have extended from the remotest period of which we have any record; and on the other hand, that where continents now exist, large tracts of land have existed, subjected no doubt to great oscillations of level, since the earliest silurian period.

claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.label: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world
claims.statement: The forms of marine life change almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense, throughout the world, so that formations in distant regions under different climates can be correlated by their fossils.
claims.quote: Scarcely any palæontological discovery is more striking than the fact, that the forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world.

claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.label: Soft-bodied organisms and remains on non-depositing sea floor are not preserved
claims.statement: Wholly soft-bodied organisms are not preserved as fossils, and shells and bones decay and disappear where they lie on parts of the sea floor where sediment is not accumulating, so the fossil record is strongly biased.
claims.quote: No organism wholly soft can be preserved. Shells and bones will decay and disappear when left on the bottom of the sea, where sediment is not accumulating.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.label: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
claims.statement: All living things have much in common in their chemical composition, germinal vesicles, cellular structure, and laws of growth and reproduction, as shown even by the same poison often affecting plants and animals similarly.
claims.quote: Nevertheless all living things have much in common, in their chemical composition, their germinal vesicles, their cellular structure, and their laws of growth and reproduction.

claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
claims.statement: Although oceanic islands have few species, the proportion of their species that are endemic (found nowhere else) is often extremely large relative to their area, as expected if occasional colonists arriving in a new isolated district are especially liable to modification.
claims.quote: Although in oceanic islands the number of kinds of inhabitants is scanty, the proportion of endemic species (_i.e._ those found nowhere else in the world) is often extremely large.

claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
claims.statement: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).
claims.quote: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country

claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claims.statement: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.
claims.quote: in both cases we see the cell-walls everywhere meeting, by threes, at angles of 120°, irrespective of the size of the individual cells: whose relative size, on the other hand, determines the _curvature_ of the partition-walls.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.label: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
claims.statement: Within a species, cones with a given parastichy arrangement are nearly equally divided between right-handed and left-handed spiral directions (e.g. 224 versus 243 among 467 Norway spruce cones).
claims.quote: In each case they were nearly equally divided as regards direction; for instance of the 467 cones shewing the five-eight arrangement, the five-series ran in right-handed spirals in 224 cases, and in left-handed spirals in 243.

claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression
claims.statement: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).
claims.quote: It was by observing, with the help of very careful measurement, this continued proportionality, that Moseley was enabled to verify his first assumption, based on the general appearance of the shell, that the shell of Nautilus was actually a logarithmic spiral, and this demonstration he was immediately afterwards in a position to generalise by extending it to all the spiral Ammonitoid and Gastropod mollusca

claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°
claims.statement: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.
claims.quote: the constant angle is in the neighbourhood of 80°; and hence also that, in all the ordinary Ammonitoid shells, and in all the typically spiral shells of the Gastropods, the constant angle is also a large one, being very seldom less than 80°, and usually between 80° and 85°.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.label: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
claims.statement: Phyllotactic parastichy numbers vary with the size of the whole structure, as in sunflower discs where one species may show 34/55, 55/89 or even 89/144 rows.
claims.quote: The arrangement, as we have seen, is apt to vary when the entire structure varies greatly in size, as in the disc of the sunflower.

claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.label: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch
claims.statement: The cannon-bones of the ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only in relative length and breadth: at equal length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's.
claims.quote: In other words, the main (and perhaps the only) difference between the two bones is simply that that of the sheep is elongated, along the vertical axis, as compared with that of the ox in the relation of 3/2.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.label: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
claims.statement: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.
claims.quote: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.

claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.label: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth
claims.statement: Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.
claims.quote: then the value of _k_, according to whether it varies or remains constant, will tell us at once whether there has or has not been a tendency to gradual alteration in the general form.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
claims.statement: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
claims.quote: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
claims.statement: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
claims.quote: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
